case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 05.10.2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2294 of 2009).
full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha CJ. This appeal by leave is directed from a judgment of the High Court Division which has affirmed the judgment of the lower appellate court. The appellate Court reviewed the judgment of the trial court.

2. Short facts are as under:

<u>3. Plaintiff instituted other Class Suit No.44 of 1995 for partition on declaring nullity of a deed against the appellant Md. Shamsul Haque and others. Plaint case in short is that on Md. Chulai was the original owner of 2.07 acres of land by purchase from one Sattar Mia by kabala dated 18th April, 1952. Said Md. Chulai died leaving 06 sons, wife Sakhina and another wife Rabeya who died during his life time. Three sons of Md. Chulai namely Md. Rawshan, Md. Asgor and Md. Sabdar through Chulai's predeceased wife rabeya sold out their entire 7 (seven) anal share of 90 decimals to one Min Uddin and Akbar by registered kabala dated 13th December, 1972. Said Alim Uddin and Akbar subsequently sold the said 90 decimals of land to the defendant Shamsul Haque in 1988. The remaining 1.17 acres of land remained in the possession of Chuli's other three sons Md. Jabbar, Md. Sattar Mia and Md. Abbas and wife Sakhina Khatun. Subsequently Md. Abbas died unmarried and his other two full brothers Md. Jabbar and Sattar Mia and mother Sakhina Khatun inherited his share. While Md. Jabbar, Md., Sattar Mia and their mother Sakhina Khatun were in possession of their 1.17 acres of land, they came to know in the middle part of 1994 that 06 decimals land out of their 1.17 acres were acquired by the government for the purpose of construction of a bypass road and that the defendant Shamsul Haque, by creating a false deed was trying to receive the compensation money Md. Jabbar, Md. Sattar and their mother then procured the certified copy of the deed and confirmed that Shamsul, Haque created the deed by false personation.</u>

4. Thereafter Md. Jabbar, Md. Sattar,  Mia and their mother Shakhina Khatun tiled the Suit in respect of their 1.17 acres of land and also for declaration to the effect that the deed 5;08.2008 in respect of their 1.17 acres of land is forged and not binding upon them.

5. Defendant No.1 (defendant) Shamsul Haque contested that suit by filling written statement. His case is that the plaintiffs sold said 1.1.7 acres of land to him in the year 1974 at a consideration of taka 2000/-and delivered possession; that though a sale deed was executed on 25,08.1974, it could not have been registered for want of necessary permission of the government which was necessary during the relevant time for transferring 'Bihari refugess' land that after withdrawal of that restriction, the deed was registered in favour of the defendant and that the defendant has been possessing this 1.17 acres of land for more than 20 years by exercising his right little and interest therein.

<u>6. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the defendant acquired a good title by adverse possession act that the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs in the suit land extinguished. The lower appellate court decreed the suit and the High Court Division has affirmed the judgment. Leave was granted to consider as to whether the High Court Division is justified in affirming the judgment of the appellate court negating the claim of adverse possession by the defendant in the suit land.</u>

7. Though the plaintiff's claim partition and entitlement of compensation money assessed by the Government in L.A. Case No. 69 of 1993-94 the only point requires to be considered is whether the defendant has acquired title b adverse possession in the suit land. It the defendant's plea of adverse possession is established, the plaintiffs cannot get a decree as prayed for.

8. There is no dispute that the plaintiffs entered into an agreement for sale of the suit land with the defendant on 25th May, 1974, but ultimately they did not execute a sale deed. Defendant claimed that the plaintiffs had executed a sale deed on 5th July 1980 but the courts below disbelieved the defendants claim which clear findings that the defendant had created the deed by false personation. Taking these admitted Nets into consideration let us consider whether the defendant can claim adverse possession in the suit land to the basis of the possession taken in pursuance of the execution of the agreement dated 25th May, 1974.

<u>9. There is no dispute that a person cannot claim title by adverse possession in the land in dispute on the basis of an agreement even if his possession exceeds over the statutory period. To constitute title by adverse possessions, the claimant must prove his hostile possession over statutory period to the knowledge of the real owner. The High Court Division, Therefore, has rightly observed, that to constitute adverse possession, One must be in possession for the statutory period openly, in assertion of his own title as owner and denying the title of the true owner, and such open hostile possession, under claim of ownership, must be to the knowledge of the true owner; mere possession without the necessary ingredients of adverse possessions however long continued, does not and cannot ripen into title by adverse possessions ". In talking the above views it has relied upon the case of Dalimunessa Bewa V. Md. Hashmat Ali. 61 DLR (AD) 8.</u>

10. The High Court Division held that though the defendant is in possession of the suit land for more than 20 years, he is not in possession as of right with a notorious hostile claim of exclusive title in arriving at such finding; the High Court Division has not assigned any reason on appraisal of the materials on record. The plaintiffs have admitted the defendant's possession of the suit land over 20 years, but according to them, the defendant was their borgader. The plaintiffs. However failed to prove their claim of giving borga cultivation. They led no legal evidence in support of their such claim. In the absence of legal evidence, the court may draw adverse inference against the assertion of claim under the rules of evidence.

11. The trial court on assessment of the evidence on record observed that the plaintiff’s witness (P.W.!) admitted that since 1994 the defendant had stopped giving the usufructs of the suit land. This is the solitary evidence adduced on behalf of the plaintiffs did not adduce any other evidence in support of giving borga cultivation of the suit land to the defendants. Therefore, the trial court has rightly held that the plaintiffs could not substantiate their claim by producing witness of giving borga cultivation to the defendant. It held that P.W.1 had admitted about the execution of unregistered deed in favour of the defendant.; that he failed to prove his plea of borga cultivation of the suit land; that the defendant has proved possession of payment of rent and mutation of his name in respect of the suit land; that the plaintiffs have failed to give any explanation for non-payment of rent; that this fact proved that the plaintiff's sold the suit land by an unregistered deed and that the plaintiffs title in the suit land extinguished by advice possessions. These findings are in conformity with law and we find nothing wrong in the conclusions arrived by the trial court.

12. The court of Appeal below notice that the plaintiffs had failed to give any explanation for non-payment of rent and held that this non-payment' of rent proved that the plaintiffs sold the suit land by an unregistered deed; that the defendant on payment of consideration money of the suit land has been in possession but that his claim of hostile possession has not been established. In arriving at such conclusion, the court of appeal below has not assigned proper reasons despite that it has found that the defendant has been in possession on payment of the sale price of the suit land to the plaintiff. It seemed that the court of appeal below was confused on the question of accrual of title by adverse possession.

<u>13. If the possession is actual, open, uninterrupted, notorious, exclusive and continuous over a statutory period, it confers an indefeasible title upon the possessor. The extent of the title acquired by adverse possession depends on the extent of the claim or right under which possession is obtained and kept, To constitute possession in the claim of the possessor must of be effectively realised in the facts, It is sufficient if the possession is overt without any attempt of concealment. That possession to the extent to which it is capable of demonstration must be hostile, notorious and exclusive to make it adverse and will only extend to the land in actual occupation of the wrong doer. All these elements of hostile possessions are present in this case and the defendant has been able to prove it by oral and documentary evidence, The trial Court has rightly held the extinguishment of plaintiff's title by adverse possession.</u>

14. The High Court Division in the Premises has committed error of law ignoring those elements and thereby committed fundamental error in affirming the judgment of the appellate court in failing to consider that the initial onus lies upon the plaintiffs that the defendant is in possession as borgadar of the plaintiffs. If the plaintiffs claim is not substantiated by legal evidence, the court can draw adverse inference against them. The plaintiffs have miserably failed to substantiate their claim and they have not adduced any iota evidence in this regard. On the other hand the defendant is claiming hostile title against the plaintiffs by proof of oral and documentary evidence. Though he entered possession by execution of an agreement, according to him he has purchased the suit land on payment of the sale price. His positive claim is that as there was restriction for selling land of non-Bengali citizens, the deed could not have been registered. The court below concurrently found in favour of the defendant. Admittedly the defendant in assertion of his right has mutated his name and has been paying rent to the government and possessing the suit land to the knowledge of the plaintiffs since 1974 claiming as owner.

15. This possession of the defendant in assertion of his right is no doubt to be treated as hostile possession to the knowledge of the true owners. The plaintiffs are totally silent why they did not take any step for eviction of the defendant had he been a borgadar under them even after knowing that the defendant has mutated his name in the record-of-right and has been paying rent. Therefore, the court of appeal below wrongly disbelieved the claim of adverse possession by the defendant or in the alternative, it can be said that the court of appeal below has failed to comprehend the accrual of title by adverse possession in a disputed land. The High Court Division committed similar error in affirming that judgment. The defendant has been possessing the suit land as of right adversely to the knowledge of the plaintiffs for 20 years. He has mutated his name and has been paying rent throughout this period. If this act of possession in assertion of right is not matured into title, what else will create title by adverse possession? Therefore, the trial court is perfectly justified in dismissing the suit.

<u>16. The High Court Division has totally overlooked the facts-proved by the defendant in support of his claim of hostile possession and on misconception of law it has affirmed the judgment of the court of appeal below. The case considered by the High Court Division squarely supports the case of the defendant. The High Court Division misconstrued the decision in failing to consider that in that case, it has been held that if there is a complete ouster by asserting hostile title the plaintiff's title is extinguished, inasmuch as, he has lost his title by the acts of the defendant who having been in possession denying the plaintiff's title openly.</u>

17. The appeal, is therefore, allowed without any order as to costs.

End.
